# Bhaddasālajātaka (Ja 465)

**ID:** Ja 465
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Bhaddasālajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Lucky Sal
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja465
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul11.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhaddasālajātaka* (Ja 465) is a birth story set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning the duty of doing good to one’s kith and kin [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as the benevolent spirit of a magnificent sāla tree (*bhaddasāla*) in a royal park [Appleton 2012; UNDV Conference 2009]. When a king decides to cut down the giant tree to fashion a palace column, the deity dissuades the monarch from felling it by pleading for the preservation of his dwelling and the younger saplings surrounding it, whom he describes as his children [Appleton 2012; Schmithausen 1991]. Modern scholars frequently discuss this tale for its bearing on early Buddhist perspectives on plant sentience and tree deities [Appleton 2012; Schmithausen 1991].

The text's extensive introductory story of the present (*paccuppannavatthu*) recounts the massacre of the Śākyan clan by King Viḍūḍabha of Kosala [Bareau 1982; Hazra 2002; Moore 2016]. Viḍūḍabha was born to King Pasenadi and Vāsabhakhattiyā, a slave woman's daughter whom the proud Śākyas had dishonestly provided in lieu of a pure-blooded Śākyan princess [Moore 2016; Sujato 2011]. Upon learning of the deception, Viḍūḍabha sought revenge and slaughtered the Śākyas, an event that the Buddha famously explains as communal or group karma resulting from a past collective offense when the Śākyas poisoned a river [Holt et al. 2003; McDermott 1976].

Curated parallels cataloged by SuttaCentral include four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records 11 matching segments shared between the canonical verses and the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), with the most extensive match spanning segments 7.1–9.4 [DharmaNexus]. Outside the Jātaka collection, the Viḍūḍabha narrative preserved in the introductory material corresponds closely to the *Vidūdabhavatthu* of the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Hazra 2002; Holt et al. 2003; McDermott 1976]. Parallel versions of the Śākyan massacre appear across the *Vinaya* collections of the Mahīśāsakas, Dharmaguptakas, and Mūlasarvāstivādins, in the *Ekottara-āgama*, Kṣemendra’s *Avadānakalpalatā* (*Vidūḍakāvadāna*), and early Buddhist relief carvings at Bhārhut [Bareau 1982; Hazra 2002; McDermott 1976; Radich 2011].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§7.1–9.4 ↔ §1448_3–1455)

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for Ja 465 (Lucky Sal) — Supplied the canonical acronym, setting blurb, title, and translation count.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse database (Ja 465) — Identified Pali text reuse matches with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā.
- [Appleton 2012] Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories (2012) — Discussed the tree deity's connection to the sāla tree and the link to the Śākyan massacre narrative.
- [Bareau 1982] André Bareau, 'Le massacre des Śākya' (1982) — Surveyed the introduction to the Bhaddasāla-jātaka among textual witnesses for the Śākyan massacre.
- [Hazra 2002] Kanai Lal Hazra, Buddhism and Buddhist Literature in Early Indian Epigraphy (2002) — Documented Viḍūḍabha's destruction of Kapilavastu and correspondence with the Dhammapadaṭṭhakathā.
- [Moore 2016] Matthew J. Moore, Buddhism and Political Theory (2016) — Summarized the narrative of Pasenadi, Vāsabhakhattiyā, and Viḍūḍabha in Jātaka 465.
- [UNDV Conference 2009] UNDV Conference Volume, Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis (2009) — Noted the depiction of the sāla tree as the Bodhisatta's dwelling.
- [Holt et al. 2003] John Clifford Holt, Jacob N. Kinnard, Jonathan S. Walters (eds.), Constituting Communities (2003) — Cited the Buddha's explanation of collective karma in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka for the Śākyas' death.
- [Radich 2011] Michael Radich, How Ajātasatru Was Reformed (2011) — Compared the presentation of Viḍūḍabha and the Śākyans with parallel Vinaya and Avadāna traditions.
- [McDermott 1976] James P. McDermott, 'Is There Group Karma in Theravāda Buddhism?' (1976) — Outlined the four principal cross-tradition versions of the Viḍūḍabha story and its Bhārhut representation.
- [Schmithausen 1991] Lambert Schmithausen, The Problem of the Sentience of Plants in Earliest Buddhism (1991) — Analyzed the tree deity's conception of the sāla tree as its body and saplings as children.
- [Sujato 2011] Bhikkhu Sujato, White Bones Red Rot Black Snakes (2011) — Discussed the narrative context of Vāsabhakhattiyā and cited the Pali text at Jātaka IV 148.
